extracted.intended_audience: general readers, fans and researchers of television/comedy production (people researching The Eric Andre Show or surreal/prank talk-show production)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and descriptive criteria for producing or evaluating episodes in the vein of The Eric Andre Show: a deconstructed late-night/prank sketch format emphasizing surrealism, discomfort-based interviews, season-specific visual themes, and risky stunt work. Covers episode structure, interview tactics, production/standards constraints, and editing/technical choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episode opening and set-destruction premise
rubrics_metrics.description: Each episode opens on the show's main set: a standard talk-show set-up with a desk, a chair, and some decor. The show's announcer declares "Ladies and gentlemen, it's The Eric Andre Show!" and the opening song begins to play. During this time, André runs onto set and destroys the backdrop, desk, and various furnishings around him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stagehands swiftly remove the broken furniture and replace it with identical pieces; the co-host usually walks in at this time. The violent/destructive opening is a recurring structural device that sets the tone for the episode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monologue style — black comedy and surrealism
rubrics_metrics.description: Monologues incorporate black comedy and surrealism. While he struggles to perform, his monologue usually turns defensive and aggressive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monologue material should lean into aggression, absurdism and discomfort rather than polished late-night delivery; use surreal or shocking images to destabilize expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episode composition: mix of elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodes are typically a mix of surreal celebrity interviews and short sketches, candid camera footage, and non sequiturs, usually focused on André's absurd behavior in regular settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interleave sketch and man-on-the-street pieces with interview segments; maintain a chaotic, fast-moving rhythm to reflect the show's aesthetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: End-credit performer usage
rubrics_metrics.description: At the end, a performer of some type plays over the ending credits. Ending performances are usually parodies of amateur acts common to public-access television, while other times they are real musicians playing their own songs with heavy twists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the end-credit slot for a final surreal or subversive musical/performative joke (examples: hardcore band wearing shock collars; opera singer with a rapper as hype man).

rubrics_metrics.name: Seasonal stylistic cohesion
rubrics_metrics.description: André has expressed that each season of the show is shot with a unique style in mind, intended to be thematically cohesive while remaining distinct from other seasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design a clear, season-long visual and thematic motif (e.g., vintage dark for season 1, tropical plants/upbeat for season 3, 'dystopian Eraserhead' for season 4, vibrant decorations/green screen for season 5) and carry it through episodes to create a distinct season identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deconstruction rather than spoof
rubrics_metrics.description: Co-director Kitao Sakurai eschewed labelling the show as a spoof, saying ... "I think it's more of a deconstruction, an alternate reality talk show rather than a spoof. I think that the interviews that we have with real people and celebrities have their own value that goes beyond spoof."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to reveal or subvert talk-show conventions rather than simply parodying them; create situations that produce authentic, revealing reactions from guests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview tactics: provoke discomfort and use exhaustion
rubrics_metrics.description: Co-director Kitao Sakurai described season 3's interview methods as "Vietcong interrogation tactics." "We almost always use the first moment of an interview," said co-director Andrew Barchilon, "And then we skip to the end, when they're exhausted and confused. That's where the gold is."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use surprising/prank elements (e.g., rotten clams under seats, heat ducts, deliberately uncomfortable studio conditions) and editing to capture guests' initial and exhausted/confused reactions; prioritize moments of authentic discomfort as comedic payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of impersonators vs real guests and guest-selection strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Guest stars appear throughout the show, with a number of them (mainly in the first season) being faked with impersonators or random people. From seasons 2 to 6, more actual celebrities appeared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to use real celebrities, impersonators, or unsuspecting public figures depending on the segment's goals; earlier seasons used fake guests to create confusion, while later seasons leaned more on real celebrity reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical/production choices to augment discomfort
rubrics_metrics.description: The studio space is not airconditioned. André said this was because the studio's airconditioning was too loud to run while filming, but that it had the added effect of making the guests feel uncomfortable, in line with the show's theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make deliberate technical choices (lighting, camera format, sound, ambient conditions) that serve the comedic intent; accept technical trade-offs if they enhance guest unease or stylistic aims (e.g., switching to HD in season 2 changed presentation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing approach: heavy editing and selecting 'gold' moments
rubrics_metrics.description: André commented that filming on a live-to-tape format is 'kind of difficult' and 'I don't think I'd do that again. [...] I think you can fit in more jokes per square inch in something that's heavily edited.' Co-director: 'We almost always use the first moment ... and then skip to the end.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor heavy editing to concentrate jokes; use temporal jumps to juxtapose initial and concluding reactions; editing is key to creating the intended surreal/comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards, practices and content limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Eric Andre Show did receive notes from 'Standards and Production' at Adult Swim, particularly regarding suicide, drug use and insulting specific deities: André commented that 'I can curse out God, but I can't curse out Jesus'. Adult Swim had flagged graphic or explicitly staged bodily-harm sketches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate and accommodate network standards and legal sensitivities when planning extreme or graphic bits; expect notes and be prepared to modify staging or depiction (e.g., implied vs explicit bodily harm).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal/consent and permit constraints for hidden-camera/street segments
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of the difficulties with gaining consent under California's regulations, some of the impromptu and hidden camera sketches had to be re-recorded in New York City. Man-on-the-street segments sometimes required permits and could attract law enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check local consent laws and permit requirements before filming hidden-camera or public-street segments; be ready to re-record segments or relocate shoots to comply with regulations and avoid legal risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk management and stunt feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Planned scenes were sometimes not shot due to safety/cost concerns (e.g., an underwater sequence too expensive/time-consuming; a manhole stunt warned of toxic gasses). André suffered injuries during production (concussions, stitches) and the production risked arrests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh stunt ambition against safety, cost and logistics; secure appropriate safety measures and permits (e.g., Hazmat suits, stunt performers) and be prepared to cancel or adapt sequences that endanger cast/crew.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of shock/graphic practical effects vs implied depiction
rubrics_metrics.description: A planned scene where 'I shit so hard that my organs fall out of my anus' was flagged by standards: 'He can shit so hard that organs fall out of his anus, but he can’t make it look like he’s intentionally doing it'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using gross-out or shock comedy, prefer implication or careful staging over explicit, realistic portrayal if network standards prohibit explicit depiction; creative practical effects and implication can achieve the intended shock without violating rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect and incorporate controversy as part of reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Guests have walked off, been angered, or later complained about editing; the show has been characterized as 'hilarious, obnoxious' and 'a deconstruction' of talk shows and has drawn comparisons to Andy Kaufman and Tom Green.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate mixed critical and public responses; consider controversy an inherent risk/instrument of the format and plan PR/response strategies accordingly.
